common_name: Markham's Pink Clematis (Double Dusky-Pink Macropetala Clematis)

planting.note: Plant container stock in spring with the crown a couple of inches below the soil surface, keeping roots cool and shaded; Markham's Pink is a compact, early-spring-blooming macropetala clematis suited to smaller supports and needs no regular pruning.

directions: Plant with roots shaded and cool while the finely divided foliage climbs into full sun to light shade on a small trellis, obelisk, or fence. Markham's Pink bears nodding, fully double, dusky rose-pink bell-shaped flowers in mid-spring, each with a mass of paler inner staminodes, followed by fluffy silvery seed heads that persist into summer. Like other macropetala types it flowers entirely on the previous year's growth, so it needs no regular pruning beyond removing dead or damaged stems and shaping right after the spring bloom. Its compact habit and reliable early color have earned it the Royal Horticultural Society's Award of Garden Merit.

common_name: White Swan Clematis (Double White Macropetala Clematis)

planting.note: Plant container stock in spring with the crown a couple of inches below the soil surface, keeping roots cool and shaded; White Swan is a compact, early-spring-blooming macropetala clematis suited to smaller supports and needs no regular pruning.

directions: Plant with roots shaded and cool while the finely divided foliage climbs into full sun to light shade on a small trellis, obelisk, or fence. White Swan bears nodding, fully double, pure white flowers with long, twisted sepals from spring to early summer, followed by decorative cream seed heads that turn fluffy and silvery-grey with age. Like other macropetala types it flowers entirely on the previous year's growth, so it needs no regular pruning beyond removing dead or damaged stems and shaping right after the spring bloom. Its clean white color and compact habit make it a good companion for spring bulbs on a small support.

common_name: Pamela Jackman Clematis (Nodding Deep Blue Alpine Clematis)

planting.note: Plant container stock in spring with the crown a couple of inches below the soil surface, keeping roots cool and shaded; Pamela Jackman is a compact, early-spring-blooming alpine clematis suited to smaller supports and needs no regular pruning.

directions: Plant with roots shaded and cool while the divided lime-green foliage climbs into full sun to light shade on a small trellis, obelisk, or fence. Pamela Jackman bears solitary, nodding, deep blue flowers to about 3 inches wide with a delicate white inner skirt and white stamens from mid- to late spring, occasionally repeating in late summer, followed by fluffy seed heads. Like other alpina types it flowers on the previous year's growth, so it needs no regular pruning beyond removing dead or damaged stems and shaping right after the spring bloom. Its compact habit and rich blue color have earned it the Royal Horticultural Society's Award of Garden Merit.

common_name: Broughton Star Clematis (Semi-Double Rose-Pink Fragrant Montana Clematis)

planting.note: Plant container stock in spring with the crown a couple of inches below the soil surface, keeping roots cool and shaded; Broughton Star is a vigorous spring-blooming Clematis montana selection needing a large, sturdy support.

directions: Plant with roots shaded and cool while the bronze-tinted foliage climbs into full sun to light shade on a large, sturdy support such as a pergola, fence, or mature tree. Broughton Star produces a heavy spring flush of fragrant, semi-double, plum-pink flowers with twisted sepals covering the vigorous vine, a distinctive sport of the species with a fuller, rosette-like bloom than typical montana types. It flowers on the previous year's growth, so prune only right after bloom to control size, never in winter or spring, which would remove the coming display. Its large ultimate size makes it best suited to a large property where it can cover a substantial structure rather than a small garden bed.

common_name: Mary Rose Clematis (Double Grey-Purple Viticella Clematis)

planting.note: Plant container stock in spring with the crown a couple of inches below the soil surface, keeping roots cool and shaded; Mary Rose is a viticella-type clematis that blooms on new growth and can be cut back hard each late winter.

directions: Plant with roots shaded and cool while the vine climbs into full sun on a trellis or through a shrub. A rediscovered old form of viticella, thought to date to the sixteenth century and reintroduced under the name Mary Rose, it bears fully double, rosette-like flowers in muted grey-purple with four to six broad outer sepals surrounding a cluster of smaller inner ones, from midsummer into early fall. As a viticella-group clematis it flowers on the current season's growth, so the entire vine can be cut back hard to about a foot from the ground in late winter, avoiding the guesswork of pruning old-wood types. Its unusual double, antique-looking flowers make it a conversation piece among viticella cultivars.

planting.note: Plant container stock in spring with the crown a couple of inches below the soil surface, keeping roots cool and shaded; Abundance is a viticella-type clematis that blooms on new growth and can be cut back hard each late winter.

directions: Plant with roots shaded and cool while the vine climbs into full sun on a trellis or through a shrub. Abundance bears open, bell-shaped flowers with four broad wine-red sepals, creamy-green filaments, and yellow anthers, produced in great profusion from midsummer through early fall. As a viticella-group clematis it flowers on the current season's growth, so the entire vine can be cut back hard to about a foot from the ground in late winter, avoiding the guesswork of pruning old-wood types. Its deep red color and free-flowering habit make it well suited to scrambling through roses or an early-blooming shrub.

planting.note: Plant container stock in spring with the crown a couple of inches below the soil surface, keeping roots cool and shaded; Silver Moon blooms on both old and new wood, so light pruning after the first flush rather than a hard cutback preserves the most flowers.

directions: Plant with roots shaded and cool while the vine climbs into a site with morning sun and some afternoon shade, since intense all-day sun can bleach the pale flower color. Silver Moon produces large, luminous, pale lavender-silver flowers to about 6 inches wide, paler along the central veins of each sepal, with creamy-white anthers, from early summer to early fall. It flowers on old wood in late spring with a lighter rebloom on new growth later in the season, so pruning should be light, removing only dead or weak stems in late winter rather than cutting the whole vine back hard. Its rare silvery-mauve color and Award of Garden Merit make it a distinctive choice among large-flowered clematis.

common_name: Pagoda Clematis (Nodding Whitish Mauve-Pink Viticella-Group Clematis)

planting.note: Plant container stock in spring with the crown a couple of inches below the soil surface, keeping roots cool and shaded; Pagoda is a viticella-group clematis that blooms on new growth and can be cut back hard each late winter.

directions: Plant with roots shaded and cool while the vine climbs into full sun on a trellis or through a shrub. Pagoda bears small, nodding, bell-shaped flowers with strongly recurved, whitish sepals margined and veined in mauve-pink and centered with yellow stamens, produced from midsummer into early fall. As a viticella-group clematis it flowers on the current season's growth, so the entire vine can be cut back hard to about a foot from the ground in late winter, avoiding the guesswork of pruning old-wood types. Its distinctive reflexed, lantern-like flowers set it apart from other small-flowered clematis on a fence or scrambling through a shrub.
